description: This cluster is the largest one (502 documents). It encloses topics related to ‘Accountability,’ ‘Public sector,’ and ‘Performance measurement.’ This cluster summarizes 36 years of FAM’s laborious work to uncover singularities of accounting in the public sector, explore its widespread implementation in many public areas, criticize various approaches, propose modernization agenda, and shed light on administrative and governmental efficiency measurements. It discusses reforms and possible future developments beyond NPM under different theoretical lenses such as instrumental, cultural, and institutional environmental features. For instance, Hyndman and Lapsley (2016) showed that NPM prompted the interest of stakeholders worldwide since 1991, including scholars, policymakers, and practitioners. In response to 2010–2015 UK. The Coalition Government’s reform decisions and the 2008–2009 global financial crisis stimulated the NPM in the UK’s government sectors. The study did not find any evidence that New Public Management is demised (Hyndman & Lapsley, 2016). Groot and Budding (2008) gathered and analyzed 105 responses to identify key aspects of NPM such as NPM effectiveness, impact on planning and control, and adoption of accrual accounting in the public sector. The outcomes revealed that NPM improved the planning and control in the public sector, while accrual accounting does not support the political decisions. Arnaboldi et al. (2015) stated that public-sector managers face difficulties in measuring performance. Even so, the ongoing academic contribution to the field of the public sector, performance measurement does not provide tidy solutions to the matter. Such difficulty in measuring the performance has not dampened the scholar’s interest in investigating and assessing the public sector performance. There are significant negative consequences associated with the sloppy implementation of performance management programs in government, including adverse effects on employee morale. The lack of ready-made alternatives to achieve improvements makes this task challenging and time-consuming for public-sector executives. Tomkins and Green (1988) proposed using data envelopment analysis to measure the efficiency of public universities. Pollitt (1986) emphasized the growing and dynamic roles of all governmental departments and the importance of dynamic, performance, and oriented management to displacing older traditions of rule-following generalist administration. Laughlin (1990) pinpointed the need to understand theoretical insights concerning accountability in practice in the case of the Church of England. Ter Bogt (2004) surveyed the case of alderman in municipalities and the degree of performance information in planning and control documents and found differences related to policy fields concerning uncertainty, measurability of outputs, and knowledge of transformation processes. Lee (2008) explored the public sector’s reporting and disclosure requirements. They investigated reported information and highlighted its usefulness to transmit annual reports. Findings pinpointed the gap between needed and reported information and addressed significant concern related to nonfinancial performance.

This cluster contributes to the literature by addressing the role of trust and control in public sector settings. Some studies elaborated on NPM reforms at the level of the public sector and the causal effect on audit (Monfardini & Maravic, 2012), others explored the autonomization and governance of the public sector (Barbieri et al., 2013), while others tested the development of transparency, trust, and accountability in service delivery (English, 2018). Ellwood and Garcia-Lacalle (2015) analyzed the audit market for health service foundation trusts and mentioned the abolition of the Audit Commission in England and Wales and its replacement by the private sector regime and audit firms. In the context of public universities audit, Craig et al. (2014) showed how extensive auditing of research output by means of performance management assessment regimes motivated by an NPM mentality has damaged individual scholarship and threatened academic freedom. Though the local government has a wide variety of responsibilities, its primary duty is to provide efficient performance to the stakeholders. Internal audit and appropriate control play a critical role in maintaining effective governance (Pilcher, 2014). The introduction of accrual accounting to government entities raised complexity, fraud risks, and corruption. Results recommended introducing an efficient internal audit to mitigate the risk. Moreover, Supreme Audit Institutions (SAIs) play a vital role in public sector accountability with core duties that include overseeing the audit of public sectors’ financial, compliance, and performance efficiency. The International Organization of SAIs has provided guidelines for SAIs to consider and explain their operational importance to various stakeholders (Cordery & Hay, 2019).

This cluster demarcates the problems regarding the transferability of business accounting to the public sector and addresses compliance with the reformed accounting regulations. Some studies elaborated on governmental accounting experiences (Christiaens & Rommel, 2008) by criticizing the inappropriate transfer of the accrual accounting framework from the profit sector and the lack of attention to the political dimension, while others studied found that the symbolism of formal accounting controls was confronted by the inaccuracy and lateness of accounting reports concluding that nonfinancial controls remained the dominant mode of operational control (Jones & Dewing, 1997). In the context of the Italian local government, Steccolini (2004) found that the annual reports serve as a general report aim. They explored that voluntary disclosure is deficient, and the main purpose was to meet the legal requirement and focus on internal stakeholders. The cluster reflects on the importance of merging accounting practices with managerial decisions to embrace public sector goals and adequately report its efficiency. This basically opens the debate toward a new era of reporting standardization in the public sector spectrum and related entities. In fact, the International Public Sector Accounting Standards (IPSASs) objectives are to harmonize and standardize public sector accounting. It aims to enhance financial reporting consolidation and comparability to overcome the divergence of nationally applicable accounting standards. Nevertheless, the IPSASs have been criticized regarding three main aspects: adoption costs, lack of pressure, and incompatibility with the public sector environment (Schmidthuber et al., 2020). Thus, researchers’ interest in the fields of public sector accounting and management control has significantly increased, and the association between the management control systems (MCS) and strategy has significantly attracted scholars’ attention (Tucker & Parker, 2015).

The advent of the Internet and the evolution of new technologies helped governments to cope with the huge volume of transactions and alleviate the burden of control and monitoring. However, E-government partnership may promote or inhibit successful collaborative working that can benefit from a governance structure supporting the consistency of objectives of the partners operating within similar political and regulatory environments (Hodges & Grubnic, 2010). Pina et al. (2010) documented that e-government has positive consequences on the public sector performance and citizen satisfaction since it ameliorates processes, improves accountability, and enhances benchmarking between the public sector entities. Furthermore, some studies investigated the process of adoption of a new governance regulation in the public sector and concluded that governance should spread in society through their construction in ‘laboratories’ where effectiveness in various jurisdictions is assumed and not questioned by governance experts, accountants, and their technologies (Tremblay, 2012). Kudo (2010) described Japanese e-governance policy and found that NPM reforms utilize various strategies to manage public policies, and e-governance is a public policy that directly affects other policies and brings about change. Another facet of technology was embraced by Liu et al. (2017). They had widened the search question to tackle concerns about voluntary climate change-related reporting such as the Australian National Greenhouse and Energy Reporting Scheme (NGERS) and its impact on government-owned corporations.
